content:
Unsigned owner received bank call claiming he had chosen a plan, then next day bank said it was a mistake

Wang Fuk Court owners' first deadline for submitting acceptance of acquisition offer letters to the government ended on 30 June. Wang Chi House, with over 75% of owners willing to sell their titles, has been included in the long-term residency scheme. The government stated that as of the 16th of this month, sales and purchase agreements had been signed with 769 households.

Mr Chan, who lives on a mid-floor unit of Wang Chi House, purchased his flat in 2017 and still has around HK$2 million of mortgage outstanding. He has yet to sign and return the "acceptance of acquisition offer letter." Speaking to Pen IC last Monday (13th), he said he received a call that day from a staff member of Standard Chartered Bank, which handles his mortgage, claiming that the government had earlier informed them he had chosen "Plan B"—the option of taking the money and buying a new Home Ownership Scheme flat.

Mr Chan immediately said he had never signed or returned the acquisition letter and questioned whether a mistake had been made, wanting to verify the information. The staff member quoted his address, insisted it was a government notification, and explained the mortgage arrangements after selling his title. The staff member also said they would record Mr Chan's situation and inform their supervisor.

The following day (14th), Mr Chan received another call from the same staff member, who said that after checking with the bank and reviewing the information provided by the government, they discovered it was the bank that "got it wrong." According to the government's records, he had not chosen "Plan B," and they apologised to him.

Worried about "being represented" and lacking information, he did not respond

Mr Chan told Pen IC that he has not signed the acquisition offer letter because the authorities have yet to respond on arrangements for maintenance costs, insurance compensation, and whether repairs will be carried out to allow residents to return to Wang Chi House. With too many uncertainties, he cannot decide to sell his title at this stage: "It's not like you say sell and I just sell." He believes the long-term residency scheme only allocates units by balloting, and the housing uses Modular Integrated Construction with uneven quality, which does not make selling his flat a priority.

After the earlier announcement that over 75% of Wang Chi House owners were willing to accept the acquisition, Mr Chan became suspicious. He noted that many in the neighbourhood group chat were not selling, and felt that the relevant figures were just "their own claims," but "no one knows what happens in between." He frankly said: "If they voted at the owners' meeting and announced it immediately, then I would believe it." He also worried about "being represented" and being taken out of context, so he did not respond at all.

"No matter what I decide, I still have to sell to them"

Regarding the bank's first call, Mr Chan was greatly surprised: "I never chose anything, but the government told the bank on my behalf that I had chosen Plan B." He gave a wry smile: "So I am one of that 75%. I always told people I'm not, I wondered who that 75% was—turns out I'm one of them myself, I just didn't know it after the fact."

Mr Chan stressed that the fairest way would be to vote in person at the owners' meeting and announce the results immediately. However, Hop On indicated that the meeting would not handle matters of selling titles. He suspected the authorities were "afraid that an immediate vote would leave no room for manoeuvre." He sighed that this incident made him feel even more that "no matter how I decide, in the end the government will use its methods to make me sell to them—it's just a matter of whether I sell sooner or later."

The bank's follow-up call the next day saying it was "a mistake" still could not fully dispel Mr Chan's doubts. He said: "They say what they say, I listen."

Even more reluctant to sell after the owners' meeting

Mr Chan understands the scheme will not change, but still hopes to find out whether, for Wang Chi House which has not been demolished, there is an option of repairs to allow residents to return. "Until it's officially announced, there's still a chance we could really get it repaired." He also pointed out that if the government ultimately legislates to acquire the property, he still has to sell, but if the government does not buy his title, "you still have to let me go back up to live."

An owners' meeting was held on Sunday (19th). Mr Chan questioned whether it was merely "going through the motions" and merely paying lip service, and avoided residents' concerns: "they only talk about what they want to talk about." Mr Chan said that after the owners' meeting, he is even less willing to sell his title to the government, because insurance money could have been used to repair Wang Chi House, but once the title is sold, the insurance payout would go to the government.

Housing Bureau: Cases with outstanding mortgages will be referred to banks after receiving letters

Pen IC contacted the Housing Bureau last Monday (13th) to ask whether they were aware of the incident, whether it involved an error on the bureau's part, whether there were similar cases, whether it affected the previously announced figures, and how residents' trust could be won. The Housing Bureau did not give a direct response, only replying yesterday (20th) that according to the HKMA and the Hong Kong Association of Banks' announcement in March this year, the HKMA, the Association, and the banking industry have set up a communication platform, including through the Housing Bureau-coordinated "Explanation Team," to understand the specific needs of Wang Fuk Court residents and provide suitable assistance for each case.

The bureau said it has been in close communication with the Hong Kong Association of Banks and the banks providing mortgages on Wang Fuk Court units. After receiving the duly signed "acceptance of acquisition offer letter" from an owner, the Explanation Team will, based on the mortgage information provided in the letter, refer cases with outstanding mortgages to the mortgagee bank in accordance with the personal data collection statement contained in the letter. This allows the bank to assign dedicated staff to contact the owner, helping them understand the special mortgage arrangements the industry offers to assist owners, and to provide appropriate assistance.

Standard Chartered: No comment on individual cases, handled with empathy

A Standard Chartered Bank spokesperson replied on Tuesday (14th) last week that it does not comment on individual customer cases, and that it has a dedicated team that handles affected Wang Fuk Court owner customers according to their individual needs with empathy, and ensures that customer data is properly handled.

The first batch acquisition deadline for Wang Fuk Court ended on 30 June. Financial Secretary Deputy Secretary Wong Wai-lun stated earlier that as of the 16th of this month, 1,786 households had signed and returned the "acceptance of acquisition offer letter," representing over 90% of all households. Among them, approximately 43%, or 769 households, have signed sales and purchase agreements.
